summary: Security review of 777641d + fa02c30 (climberDisplay identity fallback + username lookup on GET /api/users/search). No critical or high findings; no blocking findings. Verified independently against the live code, not the summaries: (1) the new username path is exact scalar equality `{ username: norm.username }` with no contains/startsWith/mode anywhere, and I confirmed the ONLY write path for users.username is settings route -> setUsername(normalizeUsername(raw)), so the absence of `mode: "insensitive"` on the DB filter is correct and complete rather than a latent miss; (2) requireAuth and checkRateLimit(namespace users:search, max 60, window 3600, failMode closed) run unconditionally before exactMatchFilter is ever called, and rateLimit.ts line 71 returns allowed:false on a Redis throw for failMode closed, so the new path is genuinely fail-safe; (3) normalizeUsername is a reject-never-default gate, malformed input returns {users:[]} with zero Prisma calls, and usersSearch.route.test.ts:121-129 asserts BOTH users===[] AND findFirst not called, using "bo" which is a real prefix of the fixture username (satisfies the positive-fixture rule in .claude/rules/testing.md); normalizeUsername's own reject rules (reserved, hateful, length, charset, dashes, empty) are unit-tested in tests/app/username.test.ts; (4) `id: { not: uid }` is preserved and, importantly, is written AFTER the `...filter` spread so a filter key can never override self-exclusion; (5) zero email exposure anywhere in the climberDisplay change — handle.ts touches only id + displayName, no DTO in the friend/challenge/notification path selects email, and the diff actually REDUCES data fetched (dropped `username: true` from two user selects); all 16 render sites pass the correct subject's server-derived id, and the 3 server routes pass the authenticated uid (friends, friends/accept) or the DB row's sender_id (challenge, set from uid by createChallenge) — never a request-supplied value; (6) no raw SQL introduced, no dangerouslySetInnerHTML, recipientId/receiverId still validated against a real user row inside createChallenge/sendFriendRequest transactions; (7) no CI workflow, install script, package.json, lockfile or secret touched, and a secret scan of the diff is clean. Gates re-run by me: app-lint clean, app-typecheck clean, app-test 748/748 in 8.29s, pnpm audit 3 advisories all pre-existing transitive with zero dependency changes in this diff.
goal: Adversarially verify that the username-lookup extension to GET /api/users/search preserves the exact-match anti-enumeration property, auth, and fail-closed rate limiting; that the climberDisplay identity fallback leaks no PII and attributes the correct actor; and run a general OWASP pass over the touched files.

findings.issue: VERIFIED SAFE. exactMatchFilter returns either { email: { equals, mode: "insensitive" } } or { username: <normalized string> } or null. The username branch is a Prisma scalar shorthand — exact equality. No contains/startsWith/endsWith/search/mode on the username branch, and findFirst returns at most one row, so no directory listing is possible. A caller can only CONFIRM a handle they already have.
findings.reproduction: GET /api/users/search?q=bobsmit (prefix of real username bobsmith) -> {users:[]}; the mock in app/tests/api/usersSearch.route.test.ts faithfully implements equals-vs-contains semantics so a regression to contains fails behaviorally, and the verifier proved it red by temporarily reverting the route.
findings.fix: None required. Do not widen the exactMatchFilter return type to Prisma.UserWhereInput — the narrow union is what structurally forbids a contains filter and an id key.
findings.adversarialVerification: Attack path traced end to end: the only user-controlled value reaching Prisma is norm.username, which normalizeUsername constrains to /^[a-z0-9-]{3,30}$/ with no leading/trailing dash. No wildcard metacharacter survives that charset, and Prisma scalar equality does not interpret wildcards regardless. No constructable enumeration path.

findings.issue: VERIFIED SAFE, with a fragility note. `where: { ...filter, id: { not: uid } }` places the self-exclusion AFTER the spread, so even a filter object that carried an `id` key could not override it. Today that is also guaranteed by the return type union. This ordering is load-bearing: if someone later reverses it or broadens the return type, self-exclusion becomes client-overridable.
findings.reproduction: n/a — this is a hardening observation, not an exploitable path at HEAD.
findings.fix: Optional: add a one-line comment above the spread noting that `id: { not: uid }` must stay last, so a future refactor does not reorder it.

findings.issue: VERIFIED SAFE. requireAuth runs first and returns 401 on any failure; checkRateLimit runs second, before the query string is even parsed. exactMatchFilter is called at line 72, strictly after both. There is no branch on input shape before the guards, so a username-shaped query cannot skip either. failMode remains "closed" and rateLimit.ts:71 returns allowed:false when Redis throws under that mode — genuinely fail-safe, not just nominally configured.
findings.reproduction: usersSearch.route.test.ts:131-139 mocks checkRateLimit to deny for a username-shaped query and asserts 429 + findFirst never called + objectContaining({ namespace: 'users:search', failMode: 'closed', max: 60 }).

findings.issue: VERIFIED SAFE and correctly tested per .claude/rules/security.md 'reject, never substitute a default'. normalizeUsername returns { valid: false } for empty, <3, >30, non-[a-z0-9-], leading/trailing dash, reserved (admin/official/support/staff/root/system/moderator/doomstack/theclimb) and hateful names; the route then returns {users:[]} without constructing a filter, so Prisma is never reached. No coercion, no fallback value, no wildcard. The test asserts real rejection (users === [] AND findFirst not called), not merely absence of a crash, and the loop includes "bo" — an actual prefix of the fixture username "bobsmith" — satisfying the positive-fixture requirement in .claude/rules/testing.md. normalizeUsername's own reject rules are separately unit-tested in app/tests/app/username.test.ts (reserved/hateful at :34-38, bounds at :16, charset at :22, dashes at :29, empty at :39).
findings.reproduction: GET /api/users/search?q=ab | q=has%20space | q=bob@ | q= -> 200 {users:[]}, zero Prisma calls.
findings.fix: None. Optional test nit: the route-level reject loop does not include a reserved word ("admin") or an over-30-char string; both are covered transitively by the normalizeUsername unit tests, so coverage is adequate.

findings.issue: VERIFIED SAFE. `id: { not: uid }` applies to the merged where clause and therefore to both the email and the username branch identically — it is outside the branch, not duplicated per branch, so it cannot drift.
findings.reproduction: Test at :141-148 asserts where.id === { not: 'me-1' } on a username-shaped query.

findings.issue: VERIFIED SAFE, and a net PII reduction. climberHandle/climberDisplay take only (id, displayName) — email is not a parameter and appears nowhere in handle.ts. Traced every consumer: no DTO in the friend/challenge/notification path selects email (grep for 'email' in src/db/notification.ts, friendship.ts, challenge.ts returns nothing), createNotification's push payload carries only title/body/type/notificationId, and the diff REMOVED `username: true` from the accepter and sender selects in the two friends routes, so strictly less user data is read than before. Actor attribution is correct at all 3 server sites: friends/route.ts and friends/[id]/accept/route.ts pass the requireAuth uid; challenge/route.ts passes c.sender_id, which is the DB row column that createChallenge wrote from the same uid (src/db/challenge.ts:69) — never from request input. All 16 client render sites pass the subject's own server-derived id (req.sender.id, req.receiver.id, f.user.id, c.sender.id, c.recipient.id, u.id), each mapped in src/db/friendship.ts / challenge.ts from a Prisma row.

findings.owasp: A07 Identification and Authentication Failures (identity spoofing)
findings.issue: The pseudonym namespace and the attacker-controlled display_name namespace overlap, and this diff extends that overlap onto a surface where the displayed identity drives a trust decision. climberHandle has only 16 adjectives x 16 animals x 100 = 25,600 possible outputs. display_name is user-chosen and validated only for invisible/bidi characters (sanitizeDisplayName) and hateful terms (isHatefulName) — nothing rejects a name shaped like a pseudonym. So user B can set display_name = "Swift Ibex 42" and render byte-identically to user A's fallback pseudonym in the Friend requests list, the Pending challenges list, the friends list, and the push-notification title ("Swift Ibex 42 sent you a friend request") — which is exactly where the recipient decides whether to accept. Independently, birthday collisions among genuine pseudonyms reach ~50% at roughly 190 display-name-less users, so two real users can share a handle with no attacker involved.
findings.reproduction: 1) As attacker, PATCH /api/settings {"displayName":"Swift Ibex 42"} (accepted: sanitizeDisplayName only strips control/zero-width/bidi code points, isHatefulName does not match this). 2) Observe a victim's leaderboard row or /c/<handle> to find a target whose fallback handle is "Swift Ibex 42". 3) POST /api/friends {receiverId: <third party who knows the target>}. The recipient's Friend requests row and push title both read "Swift Ibex 42", indistinguishable from the impersonated user.
findings.fix: Either (a) reject display names matching the pseudonym grammar in sanitizeDisplayName/settings (e.g. /^(Swift|Bold|...) (Ibex|Falcon|...) \d{1,2}$/i), or (b) render fallback pseudonyms with a visual marker the display-name path cannot produce, or (c) widen the handle space so collisions are negligible. software-engineer: not required for this change to ship.
findings.adversarialVerification: Downgraded from medium to low, deliberately, for three reasons and I am recording them so the next reviewer does not re-inflate it: (i) the class is pre-existing and explicitly accepted — src/lib/sanitizeName.ts's own docstring says 'Content moderation (profanity, impersonation, PII) is a separate product concern handled above this layer', and display_name has overridden climberHandle on the public leaderboard since before this diff; this change adds a surface, not a new class; (ii) this diff itself adds the strongest available mitigation, relaxing the @username sub-line gate from `displayName && username` to `username &&` at all 6 sites, so any user who has set a handle now always shows it beneath the name and is distinguishable; (iii) the impact is social engineering of a reversible, cancelable action (a friend request / challenge), with no authorization, payment, or irreversible write behind it — per context/trust.md the money-adjacent boundaries are climb scores and Stripe webhooks, neither of which is reachable from a display name.

findings.issue: Considered and dismissed: 'adding username lookup expands who an attacker can reach or enumerate'. It does not, because both prerequisites are already public without auth. src/db/climb.ts:167-174 returns `userId` AND `username` for every top free climber through the public /api/climb/leaderboard, and /c/[username] confirms handle existence unauthenticated with no rate limit at all. The new path is behind requireAuth plus a fail-closed 60/hr budget, i.e. strictly more restrictive than the pre-existing public surfaces. It also cannot be pivoted to learn an email: the select is { id, username, display_name } with no email field.
findings.reproduction: n/a — attack is already available through a cheaper unauthenticated path, so the endpoint is not the weakest link.
findings.fix: None. If handle existence is ever meant to be private, /c/[username] and the leaderboard payload are the surfaces to change, not this endpoint.

findings.issue: Pre-existing, NOT introduced by this diff, and not exploitable today. sendFriendRequest rejects when an existing friendship row has status 'blocked'; createChallenge has no equivalent check, so a blocked user could in principle still deliver a challenge notification. I looked for the write path and there is none: FriendshipStatus.blocked is only ever READ (src/db/friendship.ts:89 and the switch in app/api/friends/route.ts:85) — no endpoint or db helper sets it. Blocking is a latent, unimplemented feature, so there is no constructable attack path.
findings.reproduction: Not constructable at HEAD — no code path can put a friendship into 'blocked'.
findings.fix: Whoever implements the block endpoint must add the blocked check to createChallenge in the same change, or the first version of blocking ships with a bypass.

findings.issue: Pre-existing and untouched by this diff: friends:send (30/hr), friends:accept (30/hr) and challenge:create (20/hr) all use failMode "open", so during a Redis outage unsolicited friend/challenge traffic is unbounded, while users:search correctly uses "closed". Noting it because this diff broadens how easily a contact target is found, making the spam-adjacent limiters the relevant control. Not a regression and not in scope.
findings.reproduction: Requires a Redis outage; not triggerable by a remote attacker.
findings.fix: Product decision. If unsolicited-contact spam is a concern, flip friends:send and challenge:create to failMode "closed" in a separate change.

findings.issue: VERIFIED SAFE. No raw query interpolation introduced by this diff — the only DB change is a Prisma where-clause object. The two pre-existing $executeRaw calls (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE row locks) use tagged templates with ${id}, which Prisma parameterizes. On the client side, no dangerouslySetInnerHTML was added; every new name render is a React text child ({name}, @{username}) and therefore escaped, and display_name is additionally sanitized at write time against zero-width and bidi-override spoofing (sanitizeName.ts).

findings.owasp: A08 Software and Data Integrity Failures
findings.issue: Clean, as expected. git diff 4da539c..fa02c30 --name-only shows 16 app files plus 2 handoff JSONs: no .github workflow, no package.json, no lockfile, no install/postinstall script, no env or secrets handling. Secret scan of the full diff found only non-production test fixtures ("Bearer t", token: "tok", me@e.com in vi.mock factories). No hardcoded credential. pnpm audit reports 3 advisories, all pre-existing transitive with zero dependency changes here: deepmerge-ts <8.0.0 stack exhaustion (high) reachable only via the prisma CLI's @prisma/config at build time, never the request path; uuid <11.1.1 missing buffer bounds check (moderate) which requires the optional buf argument; fflate unzipSync ZIP64 infinite loop (moderate), not reachable from any code this diff touches.
findings.fix: None for this change. Separate maintenance: bump prisma to pull deepmerge-ts >=8.

findings.issue: isSearchable() plus a local copy of EMAIL_SHAPE is now duplicated in the web and mobile search components to mirror the server gate. This is correctly positioned as a rate-budget optimisation, not a security control — the server re-derives the filter from scratch and is authoritative, so client drift can only cost a wasted request or a missed local pre-filter, never a bypass. Confirmed by reading the route: it never trusts a client-side validity signal, only the raw q.
findings.reproduction: Calling GET /api/users/search?q=<anything> directly, bypassing the UI, still goes through requireAuth + rate limit + exactMatchFilter.
findings.fix: Optional: export the shape check from a shared lib so the two copies cannot diverge. Reviewer's call, not a security requirement.

gatesRun.name: app-test
gatesRun.detail: 81 files / 748 tests passed in 8.29s (matches verifier baseline 748/7.7s; no count drop, no >10x runtime jump)

gatesRun.name: pnpm audit
gatesRun.detail: 1 high + 2 moderate advisories, all transitive and all pre-existing (zero dependency or lockfile changes in this diff); none reachable from the changed code

feedback.message: SEC-7 (pseudonym/display_name namespace overlap) is the only finding with a real attack narrative, and I am deliberately NOT routing it back as blocking: it is a pre-existing accepted class (sanitizeName.ts's docstring defers impersonation explicitly), this diff adds its own mitigation by always rendering the @username sub-line, and the impact is limited to social engineering of a reversible friend/challenge action. Recording it so it is not rediscovered as a regression of this change later.
feedback.action: software-engineer: optional follow-up only — reject pseudonym-shaped display names, or mark fallback pseudonyms visually. Do not block this change on it.

feedback.message: The security-critical invariant of this endpoint now lives in a 12-line helper (exactMatchFilter) whose narrow return-type union — not a runtime check — is what forbids a `contains` filter and an `id` key. That is good design but it is an implicit control. A future refactor that types it as Prisma.UserWhereInput would silently remove both protections while all current tests still pass, because the tests exercise behaviour through the route, not the type.
feedback.action: reviewer: consider requiring a comment on exactMatchFilter's signature stating that the narrow union is a security control and must not be widened.

feedback.message: No authentication regression test exists for this endpoint: the test file mocks verifyIdToken to always succeed, so nothing proves a missing/invalid bearer token yields 401. The auth code is unchanged by this diff so this is not a finding against the change, but the endpoint's 401 path is currently unguarded by any test.
feedback.action: verifier (future work, not a loop-back): add one case that makes verifyIdToken reject and asserts 401 plus findFirst never called.

learnings.insight: Case-insensitive lookup on a normalized column is correct WITHOUT Prisma's `mode: "insensitive"` only if every write path persists the normalized form. For users.username that holds: the sole writer is app/api/settings/route.ts -> setUsername(normalizeUsername(raw).username), plus clearUsername(null); no migration or seed writes it. So `{ username: norm.username }` is both exact and complete. The general rule: before accepting a bare scalar equality filter as case-safe, grep every writer of that column, not just the one the diff touches — a single unnormalized writer turns an exact filter into a silent false-negative (a broken feature) and tempts the next author into adding `contains` to 'fix' it.
learnings.action: When reviewing an exact-match lookup on a normalized column, enumerate writers of that column and confirm each applies the same normalizer. Record the writer list in the review so the next reviewer does not redo it.

learnings.insight: In this repo the enumeration-resistance of a lookup endpoint must be judged against what is ALREADY public, not in isolation. src/db/climb.ts:167-174 puts both `userId` and `username` in the unauthenticated /api/climb/leaderboard payload, and /c/[username] confirms handle existence with no auth and no rate limit. So an authenticated, fail-closed, 60/hr username lookup adds zero enumeration capability. Two prior instincts (username directory-walk; expanded harassment reach) both collapse on that fact.
learnings.action: Before writing up an enumeration or reach-expansion finding on an authenticated endpoint, check the public leaderboard payload and /c/[username] first. If the same fact is already free and unauthenticated, the finding is info, not medium.

learnings.insight: Introducing a deterministic pseudonym as a fallback for a user-controlled name field creates a spoofing overlap the moment both can render in the same slot: climberHandle's 25,600-value space is fully reachable by simply setting display_name to 'Swift Ibex 42', and sanitizeDisplayName only strips invisible/bidi characters, so nothing rejects it. The risk is proportional to what the displayed identity gates — harmless on a leaderboard row, meaningful on an accept/decline row or a push-notification title.
learnings.action: When a pseudonym generator and a user-settable name share a render slot, either reject names matching the generator's grammar at the write path, or mark the generated variant visually. Also size the generator's space against expected user count — 25,600 values collide at ~50% by ~190 users.

learnings.insight: `where: { ...filter, id: { not: uid } }` is safe specifically because the self-exclusion is written after the spread and because the helper's return type is a narrow union that cannot carry an `id` key. Both properties are invisible at the call site and neither is covered by a test that would fail if they were lost — the existing self-exclusion test asserts the filter Prisma receives, which stays correct if a future filter simply doesn't include an id.
learnings.action: Treat 'user-influenced object spread into a where clause' as a review checkpoint: confirm security predicates come after the spread and that the spread's type cannot contain them.

learnings.insight: Independently re-run at the security stage: app-lint clean, app-typecheck clean, app-test 81 files / 748 tests in 8.29s (verifier baseline 748 / 7.7s — no count drop, no runtime regression), pnpm audit 1 high + 2 moderate all pre-existing transitive with 0 dependency changes in the diff. 16 app files changed, 0 schema changes, 0 CI/workflow/secret changes. Zero critical and zero high security findings; 1 low (SEC-7, non-blocking, pre-existing class), 12 info.
learnings.action: qa-acceptance: 748 tests / ~8s is the baseline. Security verdict is pass — do not loop back to software-engineer on security grounds.

learnings.insight: The verifier's critical process finding stands and I am re-flagging it rather than letting it be absorbed: this diff was already committed as 777641d/fa02c30 before review, contradicting the dispatch instruction and the software-engineer handoff's own exitCriteria.committed:false. My review was read-only and complete regardless, but 'already committed' must not be read downstream as 'already approved'.
learnings.action: Orchestrator: verify `git status --porcelain` against the handoff's `committed` claim before advancing a stage, per the verifier's suggestion. Integrator: confirm these two commits still get a real integration gate rather than being treated as merged history.
